title: Overhead, surface or drip irrigation
why: The manual has three ways to apply water: over the canopy, on the soil surface, and into a soil volume. Run the three with the same trigger and dose, so only the way of applying water differs.

title: Irrigation and nitrogen together
why: Water moves nitrate and decides how much of the fertiliser the crop can use. Irrigation against rainfed, at three fertiliser doses, shows whether more water raises the yield only when the nitrogen is there, and what it costs in nitrate below the roots.

title: When to irrigate: the trigger and the depth of the sensor
why: Irrigation starts when "soil water pressure above" is not true: the potential (cm) and the height (cm) are its two parameters. The potentials run from near field capacity to well before wilting for this soil texture; the depths stay inside the rooting depth of 100 cm.

title: How much and how fast: dose and duration
why: The water application speed is a parameter in mm/h (default 2 mm/h) and the irrigation lasts a number of hours. The pairs below keep the speed of the manual (2 mm/h) while the dose grows, so the answer is the effect of the dose and not of the speed.

title: Nitrogen fertiliser, irrigated and rainfed
why: Fertiliser is applied as an amount in kg N/ha. Scaling the rotation between half and one and a quarter of its dose, with and without irrigation, shows the dose where yield stops rising and the nitrate leached below the roots starts to climb.

title: A drier, wetter or warmer year
why: The weather file gives precipitation and air temperature to every model of the column. Scaling the rain and adding a warming to the same record shows how much the yield and the water use move with the weather, with the soil and the management unchanged.

title: The irrigation season and a limit on water
why: The irrigation of a crop is tested between a from date and a to date and can be given an amount. Start dates and a seasonal limit show how much of the yield is bought by the first and the last irrigations.

title: Which soil needs the most water
why: A horizon gets its hydraulic properties from the hypres model by default, from the sand, silt, clay, humus and bulk density. Rainfed and irrigated runs on several textures show where irrigation pays.

title: Slow or fast irrigation: a constant water flux
why: Daisy applies irrigation at a rate in mm/h, so a slow rate keeps the water in the topsoil and a fast one can run off or percolate. The rates below keep the same dose per irrigation, so only the speed of application differs.

title: Sensor depth against rooting depth
why: The tensiometer that triggers irrigation sits at one depth, while the roots take water from the whole root zone. A sensor above or below most of the roots triggers too early or too late; crossing the sensor depth with the rooting depth shows where it matters.

title: When the fertiliser is applied and how much
why: The fertilize action is placed on a date. Moving it two weeks earlier or later, at three doses, shows how much nitrate is exposed to the rain before the crop takes it up.

title: Warming with and without irrigation
why: A warmer year raises the evapotranspiration and shortens the crop cycle. Warming of 0 to 3 degrees, rainfed and irrigated, shows how much of the loss irrigation can give back.

title: Tillage and the time and form of the fertiliser
why: The tillage action (plowing, rotavation, or none) mixes the residues and the topsoil; the fertiliser is taken from the fertilizer library by name, and the date can be moved. These three decide how much nitrate is exposed to leaching.

title: Evapotranspiration model and radiation
why: Daisy can take the reference evapotranspiration from the weather file (FAO56) or compute it from the energy balance, and the radiation can be scaled. The runs show how much of the answer depends on that choice.

title: A dry summer, a dry spring or a wet winter
why: The weather component can scale the precipitation month by month (twelve factors). Taking 30 percent of the rain from the summer or the spring, or adding 30 percent in the winter, shows which part of the year matters for yield and for leaching.

title: Sorption and half-life of a chemical
why: A chemical has a sorption coefficient (K_OC, L/kg) and a decomposition rate; the two decide whether it stays in the topsoil or reaches the depth where it is counted as leached.

title: Deficit irrigation: a water limit against the trigger
why: A crop can be given a limited amount of water in the season, and irrigation starts only when the soil water pressure is below the trigger. A strict trigger with a small limit, against a lax trigger with a large limit, shows whether the same water gives more yield when it is saved for the dry spell.

title: Rooting depth of the crop
why: The crop model has a maximum rooting depth, which decides how much of the soil water and nitrate the roots can reach. Shallow to deep roots, rainfed and irrigated, show how much of a water shortage a deeper root zone absorbs.

title: The same farm under other climates
why: The weather component reads a file for one place. Running the same soil, crops and management with the weather of several places shows how much of the result belongs to the climate.

title: Tillage against fertiliser form
why: The tillage action mixes residues and topsoil; the fertilizer library holds several forms of mineral nitrogen. Crossing the two shows whether the form of the nitrogen matters more under one tillage than another.

title: The numerical settings of the bioclimate model (topic 19)
why: NoOfIntervals: Number of vertical intervals in which we partition the canopy; max svat iterations: Max number of svat iterations before giving up on cobvergence; max svat absolute difference [mm/h]: Maximum absolute difference in svat ea values for convergence. Each is varied from half to double the value the farm uses; NoOfIntervals moved the yield, water or nitrogen in the test.

title: The groundwater and the aquitard below the profile: aquitard (topic 45)
why: K aquitard [cm/h]: Conductivity of the aquitard; Z aquitard [cm]: Thickness of the aquitard. The aquitard begins below the bottommost soil horizon. Each is varied from half to double the value the farm uses; K aquitard, Z aquitard moved the yield, water or nitrogen in the test.

title: Turnover of organic matter and the mineral nitrogen it releases (topic 60)
why: K NH4 [h-1 ]: Maximal immobilization rate for ammonium; K NO3 [h-1 ]: Maximal immobilization rate for nitrate; CO2 threshold [h-1 ]: Turnover rate above which pools will contribute to 'CO2 fast'. Each is varied from half to double the value the farm uses; K NH4, K NO3, CO2 threshold moved the yield, water or nitrogen in the test.

title: Water at the soil surface: runoff and evaporation (topic 87)
why: temperature change rate [h-1 ]: Relative change of surface temperature. If you set this to a negative value, surface temperature will reflect temperature of incomming water or ponded; EpFactor [dimensionless]: The autumn value can be lower, due to muching. With a crop factor of 1.2 a combined Kc of 1.15 is reached at LAI=5. See also [Kjaersgaard et al., 2008]; ReservoirConstant [h-1 ]: Fraction of ponding above DetentionCapacity that runoffs each hour. Each is varied from half to double the value the farm uses; temperature change rate, EpFactor, ReservoirConstant moved the yield, water or nitrogen in the test.

title: The limits on the chemistry sink terms (topic 24)
why: max sink total [dimensionless]: Maximum allowed sink term as a fraction of total content. If variable timesteps are enabled, Daisy will try to scale down the timestep in; max sink solute [dimensionless]: Maximum allowed sink term as a fraction of solute content. If variable timesteps are enabled, Daisy will try to scale down the timestep; max sink secondary [dimensionless]: Maximum allowed sink term as a fraction of secondary domain content. If variable timesteps are enabled, Daisy will try to scale down the timestep. Each is varied from half to double the value the farm uses; none of them moved yield, water or nitrogen in the test, so the effect shows in the process itself.

title: Pipe drainage (topic 37)
why: L [cm]: Distance between pipes; rad [cm]: Inner radius of drain pipes. Each is varied from half to double the value the farm uses; none of them moved yield, water or nitrogen in the test, so the effect shows in the process itself.

title: The groundwater and the aquitard below the profile: static (topic 45)
why: table [cm]: Groundwater level. Positive numbers indicate free drainage. Each is varied from half to double the value the farm uses; none of them moved yield, water or nitrogen in the test, so the effect shows in the process itself.
